edges.effect_quant: The direct breast-cancer meta-analysis suggests a modest inverse association with cruciferous-vegetable intake, but the magnitude is not large and certainty remains moderate at best.
edges.mechanism: Cruciferous vegetables provide glucosinolate-derived compounds that can influence carcinogen metabolism and estrogen-related pathways. That mechanism is plausible for breast tissue, though diet-pattern confounding still makes the human effect harder to isolate cleanly.
edges.summary: The dedicated meta-analysis found that higher cruciferous-vegetable intake was associated with lower breast-cancer risk. Broader umbrella reviews of cruciferous vegetables and cancer generally left breast cancer on the favorable side of the ledger, but the signal is still modest enough to keep confidence below the top tier.
edges.caveats: Most of this evidence is observational and often depends on food-frequency questionnaires. Preparation methods, total vegetable pattern, and menopausal status may all influence the size of any true effect.

evidence.notes: Cruciferous vegetables intake is inversely associated with risk of breast cancer: a meta-analysis.

evidence.citation: Guo Chunyan et al 2024 J Food Sci
